cemc-pascal-2024-02.title: Split at zero
cemc-pascal-2024-02.body:
From $-5$ to $0$ is 5 units, and from $0$ to $6$ is 6 units: $5 + 6 = 11$.

**Answer: (D) 11**

cemc-pascal-2024-03.title: Half-turn
cemc-pascal-2024-03.body:
A $180^\circ$ rotation is a half-turn: the word ends up upside down and reads from right to left, still horizontal. That is choice (C). (Rotating $180^\circ$ clockwise or counterclockwise gives the same result.)

**Answer: (C)**

cemc-pascal-2024-03.title: Eliminate
cemc-pascal-2024-03.body:
After a half-turn the word must still be horizontal, which rules out (B), (D), (E) (tilted or vertical). (A) is unchanged, which would be a $0^\circ$ or $360^\circ$ turn. Only (C) is upside down.

**Answer: (C)**

cemc-pascal-2024-04.title: Count by weeks
cemc-pascal-2024-04.body:
July 8 and July 15 are also Wednesdays. Two days after July 15 is July 17: a Friday.

**Answer: (D) Friday**

cemc-pascal-2024-04.title: Use remainders
cemc-pascal-2024-04.body:
July 17 is $16$ days after July 1, and $16 = 2\times 7 + 2$. Two days after Wednesday is Friday.

**Answer: (D) Friday**

cemc-pascal-2024-05.title: Count exterior edges per rhombus
cemc-pascal-2024-05.body:
The first and last rhombi each have 3 edges on the outside of the figure; the four inner rhombi each have 2 outside edges. Perimeter $= 2\times 3 + 4\times 2 = 14$.

**Answer: (B) 14**

cemc-pascal-2024-05.title: Total edges minus shared
cemc-pascal-2024-05.body:
Six rhombi have $6 \times 4 = 24$ edges. Neighbouring rhombi share an edge, and there are 5 shared edges, each removing 2 from the count: $24 - 2\times 5 = 14$.

**Answer: (B) 14**

cemc-pascal-2024-06.title: Read the graph
cemc-pascal-2024-06.body:
Mon 4, Tue 12, Wed 8, Thu 0, Fri 6: total $30$. Left: $45 - 30 = 15$.

**Answer: (D) 15**

cemc-pascal-2024-07.title: Match the smallest pile
cemc-pascal-2024-07.body:
There are only 3 blue candies, so at most 3 of each colour can remain. She must eat at least $10 - 3 = 7$ red and $7 - 3 = 4$ yellow: at least $11$. Eating exactly 7 red, 4 yellow and 0 blue works.

**Answer: (C) 11**

cemc-pascal-2024-07.title: Count what remains
cemc-pascal-2024-07.body:
Leaving $k$ of each colour ($k \le 3$) means she ate $20 - 3k$ candies. This is smallest when $k = 3$: $20 - 9 = 11$.

**Answer: (C) 11**

cemc-pascal-2024-08.title: Subtract the overlap
cemc-pascal-2024-08.body:
Of the 10 with black hair, 3 wear glasses, so $10 - 3 = 7$ do not.

**Answer: (A) 7**

cemc-pascal-2024-09.title: Fraction left for the hill
cemc-pascal-2024-09.body:
$25\% = \frac14 = \frac28$, so river and forest cover $\frac28 + \frac58 = \frac78$. The hill is $\frac18$ of the trail, which is 3 km, so the trail is $8 \times 3 = 24$ km.

**Answer: (A) 24 km**

cemc-pascal-2024-09.title: Check
cemc-pascal-2024-09.body:
For 24 km: river $6$ km, forest $\frac58\cdot 24 = 15$ km, hill $24 - 21 = 3$ km ✓.

**Answer: (A) 24 km**

cemc-pascal-2024-11.title: Start with all 2s
cemc-pascal-2024-11.body:
If all 10 baskets were 2-pointers she would have 20 points. Each 3-pointer adds 1 more, and she needs 6 more points, so she made 6 three-point baskets ($6\times3 + 4\times2 = 26$).

**Answer: (B) 6**

cemc-pascal-2024-12.title: Eliminate
cemc-pascal-2024-12.body:
The primes are 11 and 13 (Karla and Levi). The only perfect square is 16 (Glen). The remaining even numbers 12 and 14 go to Hao and Julia. That leaves 15 for Ioana.

**Answer: (B) 15**

cemc-pascal-2024-13.title: Count pairs
cemc-pascal-2024-13.body:
Two lines meet at most once, so the number of intersection points is at most the number of pairs of lines: $\frac{4\times 3}{2} = 6$. Drawing 4 lines with no two parallel and no three through a point achieves 6.

**Answer: (D) 6**

cemc-pascal-2024-13.title: Add one line at a time
cemc-pascal-2024-13.body:
Start with 3 lines in general position (3 points, as in Figure 2). A fourth line can cross each of the 3 lines at a new point, adding at most 3: total $3 + 3 = 6$.

**Answer: (D) 6**

cemc-pascal-2024-14.title: Compare sums
cemc-pascal-2024-14.body:
Sum of 10 numbers: $170$. Sum of remaining 9: $144$. Removed: $170 - 144 = 26$.

**Answer: (A) 26**

cemc-pascal-2024-14.title: Think about the drop
cemc-pascal-2024-14.body:
The 9 remaining numbers average 16. The removed number pulled the average up from 16 to 17 over 10 numbers, i.e. it was $10 \times 1 = 10$ more than 16: $26$.

**Answer: (A) 26**

cemc-pascal-2024-15.title: Equilateral then isosceles
cemc-pascal-2024-15.body:
$CD = DE = EC$, so $\triangle CDE$ is equilateral and $\angle DEC = 60^\circ$. Then $\angle CEB = 180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ$. Since $CE = EB$, $\triangle CEB$ is isosceles, so $\angle EBC = \frac{180^\circ - 120^\circ}{2} = 30^\circ$.

**Answer: (A) 30°**

cemc-pascal-2024-15.title: Exterior angle
cemc-pascal-2024-15.body:
In isosceles $\triangle CEB$ ($CE = EB$), the base angles at $C$ and $B$ are equal, and the exterior angle $\angle DEC = 60^\circ$ equals their sum. So each is $30^\circ$.

**Answer: (A) 30°**

cemc-pascal-2024-16.title: Reason about the conditions
cemc-pascal-2024-16.body:
$x^2 < x$ forces $0 < x < 1$, ruling out (A), (D), (E). For $x = \frac13$: $x^2 = \frac19 < \frac16 = \frac x2$, which fails. For $x = \frac34$: $\frac x2 = \frac38 = \frac{6}{16} < \frac9{16} = x^2 < \frac{12}{16} = x$ ✓.

**Answer: (C) $\frac34$**

cemc-pascal-2024-16.title: Solve the inequalities
cemc-pascal-2024-16.body:
$x^2 < x$ means $0 < x < 1$. Then $\frac x2 < x^2$ means (dividing by $x > 0$) $\frac12 < x$. So $\frac12 < x < 1$; of the choices only $\frac34$ works.

**Answer: (C) $\frac34$**

cemc-pascal-2024-17.title: Total distance over total time
cemc-pascal-2024-17.body:
First part: $2 \times 100 = 200$ km in 2 h. Second part: 200 km at 80 km/h takes $2.5$ h. Average: $\frac{400}{4.5} \approx 88.9$ km/h, closest to 89.

**Answer: (B) 89 km/h**

cemc-pascal-2024-17.title: Why not 90
cemc-pascal-2024-17.body:
The average of 100 and 80 is 90, but Melanie spends more time (2.5 h) at the slower speed than at the faster one (2 h), so the average is a bit below 90: $\frac{2(100) + 2.5(80)}{4.5} = \frac{400}{4.5} \approx 88.9$.

**Answer: (B) 89 km/h**

cemc-pascal-2024-19.title: Find x, then the height
cemc-pascal-2024-19.body:
Triangle perimeter: $2(3x + 4) + 2x = 8x + 8$. Rectangle perimeter: $2(2x - 2) + 2(3x - 1) = 10x - 6$. Setting equal: $2x = 14$, $x = 7$.

So $AC = 14$ and $AB = BC = 25$. The altitude from $B$ meets $AC$ at its midpoint, so it has length $\sqrt{25^2 - 7^2} = \sqrt{576} = 24$. Area $= \frac12 \cdot 14 \cdot 24 = 168$.

**Answer: (C) 168**

cemc-pascal-2024-20.title: Best ending, best start
cemc-pascal-2024-20.body:
$25N$ is between $25\,000\,000$ and $250\,000\,000$. A multiple of 25 ends in $00, 25, 50$ or $75$; the best ending is $75$ (digit sum 12). Treat $25N$ as a 9-digit string $xyz\,dddd\,75$ (leading digit possibly 0). The middle four digits can all be 9.

The first three digits: $x \le 2$, and $x = 2$ forces $y \le 4$ (since $25N \le 250\,000\,000$), so the best is $x = 1$, $y = z = 9$: $199\,999\,975 = 25 \times 7\,999\,999$, with $N$ in range.

Digit sum: $1 + 9\times 6 + 7 + 5 = 67$.

**Answer: (C) 67**

cemc-pascal-2024-20.title: Bound the digit sum

cemc-pascal-2024-21.title: Use the middle column
cemc-pascal-2024-21.body:
The middle column contains a 1, so step (ii) was never applied to it (that would make every entry at least 2). So the middle column $1, 3, 2$ shows how many times step (i) was applied to rows 1, 2, 3: $a = 1 + 3 + 2 = 6$.

Subtracting the row contributions $1, 3, 2$ from the first column $7, 9, 8$ leaves $6$ each: step (ii) was used $3$ times on column 1. From the third column $5, 7, 6$ it leaves $4$: step (ii) used $2$ times. So $b = 5$ and $a + b = 11$.

**Answer: 11**

cemc-pascal-2024-21.title: Algebra with row and column counts
cemc-pascal-2024-21.body:
Let step (i) be used $r_1, r_2, r_3$ times on the rows and step (ii) $c_1, c_2, c_3$ times on the columns. The entry in row $i$, column $j$ is $r_i + 2c_j$.

Top-middle: $r_1 + 2c_2 = 1$ forces $c_2 = 0$, $r_1 = 1$. Then the middle column gives $r_2 = 3$, $r_3 = 2$. The top row gives $1 + 2c_1 = 7$ and $1 + 2c_3 = 5$, so $c_1 = 3$, $c_3 = 2$. (Check: row 2 is $3 + 6, 3, 3 + 4 = 9, 3, 7$ ✓.)

$a = 1 + 3 + 2 = 6$, $b = 3 + 0 + 2 = 5$, so $a + b = 11$. As a check, the table total is $48 = 3a + 6b = 18 + 30$.

**Answer: 11**

cemc-pascal-2024-22.title: Hide red cubes where they show least
cemc-pascal-2024-22.body:
In a $3\times3\times3$ cube: 1 centre cube shows 0 faces, 6 face-centre cubes show 1 face each, 12 edge cubes show 2 faces each, and 8 corner cubes show 3 faces each.

Put the 10 red cubes in the least visible spots: the centre (0), all 6 face-centres (1 each), and 3 edge positions (2 each). Red area $= 0 + 6 + 6 = 12$.

**Answer: 12**

cemc-pascal-2024-22.title: Why it can't be less
cemc-pascal-2024-22.body:
Only 7 positions show at most 1 face (1 centre + 6 face-centres), contributing at most $6$ red faces. The other 3 red cubes must go in positions showing at least 2 faces each, adding at least $6$. So the minimum is $6 + 6 = 12$.

**Answer: 12**

cemc-pascal-2024-23.title: Case on where the 4s are
cemc-pascal-2024-23.body:
A 4 must be in position 1 or 3 (or both).

- **4 in both** ($4\_4\_$): the other two digits are the 2 and the 7 in either order: $4247, 4742$ — **2 codes**.
- **4 only in position 1** ($4bcd$): the remaining three digits are a 2, a 7, and one of 1 or 6. Place 2 (3 ways), then 7 (2 ways), then choose 1 or 6 (2 ways): **12 codes**.
- **4 only in position 3** ($ab4d$): the remaining digits are a 2 (not in position 1, so 2 ways), a 7 (2 ways), and 1 or 6 (2 ways): **8 codes**.

Total: $2 + 12 + 8 = 22$.

**Answer: 22**

cemc-pascal-2024-23.title: Choose the fourth digit first
cemc-pascal-2024-23.body:
The four digits are 2, 7, 4 and one more digit $w$. By rule 4, $w \in \{1, 6, 4\}$.

- $w = 4$: the 4s fill positions 1 and 3 (the only allowed positions), and 2, 7 fill 2 and 4: $2$ codes.
- $w = 1$ or $6$: arrange $\{2, 7, 4, w\}$ with 4 in position 1 or 3 and 2 not in position 1. With 4 in position 1: $3! = 6$ arrangements of the rest. With 4 in position 3: $3! = 6$ minus the 2 with the 2 first $= 4$. So $10$ codes for each $w$, $20$ in all.

Total $2 + 20 = 22$.

**Answer: 22**

cemc-pascal-2024-24.title: Add and subtract regions
cemc-pascal-2024-24.body:
Call $w$ the area of the small quarter circle and $z$ the part of the rectangle inside the large quarter circle. Then:
- large quarter circle $= y + w + z$
- rectangle $GDCF = x + z$

So $y - x = (\text{large quarter}) - (\text{small quarter}) - (\text{rectangle})$.

Large quarter circle (radius 30): $\frac14\pi(900) = 225\pi$. Small quarter circle (radius 15): $\frac{225}{4}\pi$. Rectangle: $15 \times 30 = 450$.

$y - x = 225\pi - \frac{225}{4}\pi - 450 = \frac{675}{4}\pi - 450 \approx 80.1$.

Since this is positive, $d \approx 80.1$ and the closest integer is $80$.

**Answer: 80**

cemc-pascal-2024-24.title: Compute x and y separately
cemc-pascal-2024-24.body:
Put $C$ at the origin, $E = (-30, 0)$, $D = (0, 30)$, $F = (-15, 0)$, $G = (-15, 30)$. The rectangle is $-15 \le u \le 0$, $0 \le v \le 30$.

The large quarter circle covers the rectangle up to the arc; $x$ = rectangle minus that part. The part of the large quarter disc with $-15 \le u \le 0$ is a $30^\circ$ sector plus a right triangle with legs 15 and $15\sqrt3$: $\frac{30}{360}\pi(900) + \frac12(15)(15\sqrt3) = 75\pi + 112.5\sqrt3$. So $x = 450 - 75\pi - 112.5\sqrt3 \approx 450 - 235.62 - 194.86 = 19.52$.

The part of the large quarter disc with $u \le -15$ is $225\pi - (75\pi + 112.5\sqrt3) = 150\pi - 112.5\sqrt3 \approx 276.38$; removing the small quarter disc ($\frac{225}4\pi \approx 176.71$) gives $y \approx 99.67$.

$d = y - x \approx 99.67 - 19.52 \approx 80.1$, closest integer $80$.

**Answer: 80**

cemc-pascal-2024-25.title: Reduce to exponents
cemc-pascal-2024-25.body:
Write $a = 3^r$, $b = 3^s$, $c = 3^t$ with $1 \le r \le s \le t \le 8$. Then $\frac{ac}{b} = 3^{r + t - s}$ and $\frac{bc}{a} = 3^{s + t - r}$ always have positive exponents, so they are integers. $\frac{ab}{c} = 3^{r + s - t}$ is an integer exactly when $t \le r + s$.

Count triples with $r \le s \le t \le \min(8, r + s)$:
- $r = 1$: for $s = 1..7$, $t \in \{s, s+1\}$ (2 each), and $s = 8$: 1. Total $15$.
- $r = 2$: $s = 2..6$: 3 each ($15$), $s = 7$: 2, $s = 8$: 1. Total $18$.
- $r = 3$: $s = 3..5$: 4 each ($12$), $s = 6, 7, 8$: $3, 2, 1$. Total $18$.
- $r = 4$: $s = 4..8$: $5, 4, 3, 2, 1$. Total $15$.
- $r = 5, 6, 7, 8$: the condition $t \le r + s$ is automatic, giving $10, 6, 3, 1$.

$N = 15 + 18 + 18 + 15 + 10 + 6 + 3 + 1 = 86$.

**Answer: 86**

cemc-pascal-2024-25.title: Count the complement
cemc-pascal-2024-25.body:
The number of triples $1 \le r \le s \le t \le 8$ is $\binom{10}{3} = 120$. Subtract those with $t > r + s$, which needs $r + s \le 7$:
- $r = 1$: $s = 1..6$, $t$ from $s + 2$ to 8: $6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1$ → $21$
- $r = 2$: $s = 2..5$, $t$ from $s + 3$ to 8: $4, 3, 2, 1$ → $10$
- $r = 3$: $s = 3, 4$, $t$ from $s + 4$ to 8: $2, 1$ → $3$

Bad triples: $34$. So $N = 120 - 34 = 86$.

**Answer: 86**
